paragraphs: §1 — The alleged differentia ("creating bodies") is not the only one, and creation belongs to the Creator alone

As for this last statement, which we related on the authority of some of them, it is of manifest corruption and plain absurdity; for the one who said it pronounced a verdict and decided a matter upon a premise that is neither conceded nor agreed upon — namely his saying that the meaning by which the angels are differentiated from human beings is the creating of bodies (ikhtirāʿ al-ajsām).

This [conclusion] would only follow if there were here no differentia (faṣl) other than this one; but since there are here other differentiae, then on what basis did he decree what he decreed? For among that which differentiates the angels from human beings is that the dwelling-place of the angels is in the upper sphere, above the earth, and that there has been placed in them the power to descend upon the earth at need and to return to heaven — and that is contrary to the human being, who cannot manage to ascend even a short distance except by an instrument upon which he climbs. And of that [differentia also] is the length of [their] abiding to the end of time; and this is the definition (ḥadd) by which the logicians (al-manṭiqiyyūn) defined the angels and by which they differentiated between them and human beings — namely that the definition of the human being is that he is "living, rational, mortal," whereas the definition of the angels is "living, rational [beings who do not die]." And of that [differentia also] is [their] dispensing from nourishment by food and drink; and of that [also] is the reversal of nature (qalb al-ṭabʿ) and the like of it, of the working of miracles. And since that is as we have described, what they relied upon as a ground — that the differentia is the creating of bodies and of concrete beings (al-aʿyān) — does not follow, since the Creator (sublime and mighty) is the One who is alone in that, to the exclusion of any other.

: The "last statement" picks up the close of Bab 19, where Q reported that one of the doctrine's adherents, "wishing to indicate that from reason," argued that things are differentiated from one another by fuṣūl (differentiae) subsisting in them, and that the differentia separating angels from humans is ikhtirāʿ al-ajsām (the creating of bodies) — whence "the creator of bodies is an angel." Q's reply is a logician's one: the argument is a fallacy of the inverse — even granting that body-creation, if it were the sole differentia, would prove the creator an angel, the inference collapses once one observes that there are other differentiae, so the differentia need not be body-creation at all. : The OCR carries marginal/diacritical markers (①②③) at the points where Q invokes the logicians' definitions; they are positional, not textual, and are not rendered. : Q's list of fuṣūl (locale in the upper sphere with power of descent; perpetual duration; freedom from nutrition; power to reverse nature/work miracles) is drawn from the standard Aristotelian-Porphyrian definition by genus and differentia: human = "living, rational, mortal" (ḥayy nāṭiq mayyit), angel = "living, rational, [immortal]" (ḥayy nāṭiq, with mortal struck out). Q's point is decisive for the whole doctrine: the genuine proprium of the Creator is ikhtirāʿ (origination ex nihilo) itself, which belongs to God alone — so it cannot serve as the differentia of a creature (an angel), and the creator-angel doctrine is self-undermining. The vocabulary (ikhtirāʿ, al-aʿyān, al-ajsām) is the kalāmī apparatus of created substance.
§2 — The dilemma: is body-creation common to all the angels, or peculiar to the first angel?

2. Then they are asked, and it is said to them: Inform us — is the way of all the angels one and the same in this differentia, namely that they, all of them, create bodies; or is this differentia peculiar to the first angel alone? If the way of all of them is one and the same in this differentia, then God (exalted be His grandeur) did not create one angel only, but rather created all the angels — and they are a multitude beyond numbering, as Scripture has uttered. So this one [angel], whom you allege to be peculiar [in rank], and to be magnified and preferred above the rest of the angels — by what was he differentiated, and by what did this excellence and this peculiarity come to belong to him, when the rest are his equals in creation and in the differentia? And if his way is not the way of the rest of the angels, and this excellence — which is the creating (al-ikhtirāʿ) — belongs to him to their exclusion, then by what are the rest of the angels differentiated from human beings? And this is destructive (nāqiḍ) of what they put forward and relied upon as a ground — namely that the differentia by which the angels are differentiated from human beings is the creating.

: The OCR carries a positional marker (③) here; not rendered. : A clean two-horned dilemma. Horn 1: if creating-bodies is common to all angels (and Scripture affirms the angels are innumerable), then the doctrine's privileged "first angel" has no differentia setting him above the rest, and the claim that he is the exalted world-maker is groundless. Horn 2: if creating-bodies is peculiar to him, then the original premise — that body-creation is the differentia separating angels (as a class) from humans — is false, since the other angels would then share no differentia with humans on this account. Either way the rational argument of Bab 19 is nāqiḍ (self-contradictory). This is the same dialectical structure Q uses against the Christians' "which hypostasis created Adam?" in Bab 6 §2.
§3 — The created angel cannot ground the eternity of its maker

3. It is also said to whoever holds [the doctrine] of the angel: Inform us about the world — does it indicate that its maker is eternal (lam yazal)? If he says "yes," it is said to him: you have invalidated and destroyed what you incline to of the doctrine of the angel, since the angel that made the world is, in your view, temporally-originated (muḥdath); so if you say that the world indicates that its maker is pre-eternal (azalī), then the two statements have contradicted one another. And if he alleges that the world does not indicate that its maker is pre-eternal, he is asked about the indication of the pre-eternity of the First Creator who created the angel — for they will find no way to that, since the angel, which is a creation belonging to Him, is not observed [by us], that the indication of the pre-eternity of its maker should become plain therein.

: A reductio turning on the cosmological argument. The proof of God's existence and eternity runs from the observed contingency of the world to a pre-eternal maker. If the doctrine's adherent grants that the world proves an eternal maker, then since (on his view) the world's maker is the temporally-originated angel, he contradicts himself (an eternal thing that came to be). If he denies that the world proves an eternal maker, he saws off the branch he sits on: the only thing we observe is the world; the postulated First Creator behind the angel is unobserved (ghayr mushāhad), so there is no longer any evidentiary route to His eternity at all. The interposition of a created angel between God and the world thus destroys the very argument by which one knows God. azalī / lam yazal (pre-eternal, "ever-was") versus muḥdath (temporally-originated) is the organizing kalāmī dichotomy (cf. glossary §I).
§4 — Why delegate creation? The "loftiness" motive is self-defeating and resembles the Manichaeans

4. And it is said to them: Inform us — why did the First, Pre-eternal Creator not create the world [Himself], and why did He commit its creation to the angels whom He created? Was that [done] as an exalting and a holding-above (tarfīʿan wa-tanzīhan) of Himself, [keeping Himself] clear of creating? If that is so, then why did He create the angel? For in His creating of the angel there is an indication that He did not hold Himself above creating. So they have no answer in that except to say that He held Himself above creating the world only on account of the cause [residing] in it — the [base] fragments (al-faldhāt), the impurities, and the filth that are in it; whereas the angel, which He created — since there was in it nothing of this, but it was rather a thing of noble element and exalted substance, untainted by anything of this deficiency and defect — it was admissible for Him to create it. And this statement is of the same kind as the statement of the Manichaeans (al-Mannāniyya).

So it is said to them: this [creating] would only be something He must hold Himself above if, in His creating of [the world], He were in direct contact with it and touching it; but since He is neither in direct contact with it nor touching it, but rather creates it and makes it by His will (bi-irādatihi), He need not hold Himself above it — just as He does not hold Himself above creating the angel to which He committed that [task] and with whose deed He was content. Unless, that is, He were not content with what that angel did; and if they say that, then they allege that the world came to be without the will of the First, Pre-eternal Creator — and this statement is of the utmost corruption. So the doctrine of the angel is of that which the intellect does not permit, but rather denies and pronounces absurd.

: The adherents' only available motive for delegating creation is dualist: the material world is intrinsically base (faldhāt, "[base] fragments / lumps of matter," impurities, filth), so the transcendent God will not soil Himself by making it directly, and delegates the task to a noble intermediary. Q tags this precisely as qawl al-Mannāniyya — the doctrine of the Manichaeans (followers of Mani, Mānī), the paradigmatic dualists for the kalām heresiographers, for whom the evil material cosmos is the work of a lower or opposed principle. The label is itself a refutation by association: the creator-angel doctrine is crypto-Manichaean. : The decisive disanalogy: God creates by will (bi-irādatihi), not by physical contact (mubāshara / mumāssa). The dualist intuition that the Pure One is defiled by making the impure presupposes contact — but a creator who acts by sheer volition touches nothing, so no defilement, hence no motive to delegate. Q then closes the escape route: the only way to keep the motive alive is to say God was not content (ghayr rāḍin) with the angel's work, which makes the world arise against God's will — a blasphemous absurdity. The argument is a tidy specimen of Q's Bahshamī commitment to creation as an act of the divine irāda.
§5 — The prophetic idiom: a speaker voices what is truly God's
5. As for that which they attached themselves to from Scripture, the answer concerning it has already preceded —

[that is,] in [our treatment of] the meaning of His saying [Gen 1:27] בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ ("in our image, after our likeness"), with that which there is no need to repeat — that being in the refutation of whoever held that the Creator is a body. As for the answer concerning His saying [the angel speaking as God] וַיִּקְרָא בִשֵׁם יְיָ and His saying [to Hagar] אַרְבֶּה אֶת זַרְעֶךָ ("I will multiply your seed"), and His saying to Abraham [Gen 22:17] בשם ייָ, כִּי בָרֵךְ אֲבָרֶכְךָ וְהַרְבָּה אַרְבֶּה אֶת זַרְעֶךָ, and His saying to Jacob [Gen 28:13 / 46:3] בשם ייָ, אָנֹכִי הָאֵל אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ etc., and His saying to Moses [Exod 3:6] אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ etc. — [the answer is] that these angels, or this angel, who said these sayings, even though the outward sense of the saying and what is heard of it [suggests that] the speaker intends by it himself, yet what is [really] meant by that is the First Creator (sublime and exalted).

And there are many parallels to that in Scripture. Of that is the saying of Moses to Joshua [Deut 31:23, cited as בּדבר יְיָ] כִּי־אַתָּה תָּבִיא אֶת־הָעָם הַזֶּה ("for you shall bring this people") etc., then he says [same place] ואנכי אהיה עמך ("and I will be with you"). For Moses (peace be upon him) did not mean himself, that he would be with Joshua; rather he intended by it that God said "I will be with you" — and even though [Moses] did not state that explicitly, the one to whom it was said knew the meaning of it. The like of that is the saying of Elijah to Ahab [1 Kgs, paraphrasing כּמָא יְגַּלֵּי] יען אשר הִרְמִּיתָני מתוך העם — [where] it is not he [Elijah] who raised him up, but the Creator (mighty and exalted) is the One who raised him up, though the statement was [made] on His behalf. And the like of that also is the saying of Moses, concerning God, of His like [Deut 11:14, cited בּדבר יְיָ] כִּי־בָא לָתֵת ("[I will give] the rain of your land in its season, the early rain and the latter rain") etc., and the whole account — for the outward sense of the saying is ascribed to Moses, while the reality is that God does that. And likewise also the saying of Elijah to Ahab [1 Kgs 21:21, cited נִמְצָא כָא, כָא] הִנְנִי [מֵבִיא] אֵלֶיךָ רָעָה וּבִעַרְתִּי אַחֲרֶיךָ ("behold, I bring evil upon you and will sweep away after you"). So if it is admissible for the prophets to ascribe the outward sense of the saying to themselves, while the reality of that returns to God (exalted be His mention), then the like of that is admissible for the angels.

: The clause "the answer concerning it has already preceded" is the back-reference; the text then resumes, after the page-break, with the Gen 1:26-27 cross-reference. There is no lacuna — the connective is Q's own, and the merged OCR runs the two pages continuously. : Q first disposes of be-tzalmenu ki-dmutenu (Gen 1:26-27) by cross-reference to his earlier anti-anthropomorphism (tashbīh) refutation — exactly the same back-reference he makes in Bab 6 §2, pointing to Maqala II. He then states the governing exegetical principle for the rest of the bab: in the theophany-narratives where an angel speaks in the first person as God ("I will multiply your seed," "I am the God of your father"), the angel is the mouthpiece, and the real referent (al-maqṣūd) of the first-person speech is al-Khāliq al-awwal — God Himself. The angel's "I" is God's "I." This dissolves the doctrine's scriptural foothold without conceding that the angel is a creator. : The supporting principle is a general feature of prophetic idiom: a prophet may utter, in his own first-person voice, what is in reality God's deed and speech. Moses says "I will be with you" (Deut 31:23) but means God will be; Moses delivers the rain-promise (Deut 11:14) in the first person though God is the giver; Elijah says "I bring evil upon you" (1 Kgs 21:21) though it is God who brings it. The OCR of these citations is heavily corrupted (the diff-report logs letters_differ = yes throughout p175); the Hebrew has been restored to the Masoretic text Q is evidently citing, and the verse references supplied. Q's hermeneutical move — the outward speaker ≠ the real agent — is the philological key that defangs every "an angel/the Lord did X" prooftext.
§6 — "The Lord appeared," "the Lord rained": God acts through angelic and human agency

6. As for the account [in] [Gen 18:1] וַיֵּרָא אֵלָיו יְיָ ("and the Lord appeared to him"), and His saying [Gen 19:24] וַיְיָ הִמְטִיר עַל סְדֹם ("and the Lord rained upon Sodom"), and His saying [Gen 19:21, cited בשת, כא׳] לְבִלְתִּי הֲפֹךְ אֶת הָעִיר ("not to overthrow the city") — together with the rest of what they mentioned of this kind, such as [Gen 48:16] בשם ייָ, מַלְאָךְ הַגֹּאֵל אוֹתִי ("the angel who redeemed me"), and His saying [Exod 23:20] הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי שֹׁלֵחַ מַלְאָךְ לְפָנֶיךָ ("behold, I send an angel before you"), and His saying [Isa 63:9] וּמַלְאַךְ פָּנָיו הוֹשִׁיעָם ("and the angel of His presence saved them"), and the rest of that — [the answer is that] we do not doubt that God (blessed and exalted) sends His angels for the deliverance of a people and their succor, and for [the destruction of] a people and the perishing of a people, and for [sundry] kinds of deeds and works.

And we have also seen Him do that by the hands of human beings — and that is like the working of the signs and miracles that come to pass at the hands of the prophets, and like His saying [Judg 3:9] וַיָּקֶם יי מוֹשִׁיעַ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיּוֹשִׁיעֵם אֶת עָתְנִיאֵל בֶּן קְנַז ("and the Lord raised up a deliverer for the Children of Israel and delivered them — Othniel son of Kenaz"), and also [Judg 3:15] וַיָּקֶם יי לָהֶם מוֹשִׁיעַ אֶת אֵהוּד בֶּן גֵּרָא ("and the Lord raised up for them a deliverer — Ehud son of Gera"). And since God (mighty and exalted) does that by the hands of human beings, His doing it by the hands of the angels is the more fitting and the more admissible.

: The "the Lord appeared/rained/overthrew" verses (Gen 18-19) and the "angel" verses (Gen 48:16; Exod 23:20; Isa 63:9) are met not by the mouthpiece-principle of §5 but by agency: God genuinely sends angels to deliver, to succor, and to destroy — which no monotheist denies — but sending an agent is not delegating creation. Q clinches it a fortiori: Scripture freely says "the Lord raised up a deliverer" when the deliverer is plainly a human judge (Othniel, Ehud — Judg 3:9, 3:15); since God's acting through human agents is uncontroversial, His acting through angelic agents is all the more so. In neither case does the agent become the creator. The OCR of these citations is again corrupted (diff-report p174); restored to the MT.
§7 — "The Lord is greater than all gods": the prophets' rhetoric of wonder at idolatry

7. As for that which they relied upon as a ground from the other class — which is His saying [Exod 18:11] עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי גָדוֹל יי מִכָּל הָאֱלֹהִים ("now I know that the Lord is greater than all the gods") and what resembles it — the like of it is binding upon them with regard to the angels; for [it is] on their own view that it is inadmissible for a thing to be compared, or related, except to what is near it — [yet] the angel is, in their view, the creator of the entire world; so how is it admissible for it to be compared and related to the idols, which are inert matter and of what [men] have wrought and shaped, [mere] images of men? And Scripture employs the like of this frequently — and that is like His saying [Jer 10:6] מֵאֵין כָּמוֹךָ יי ("there is none like You, O Lord"), and [Jer 10:7] כִּי בְכָל חַכְמֵי הַגּוֹיִם וּבְכָל מַלְכוּתָם ("for among all the wise men of the nations and in all their kingdoms [there is none like You]"); then he says after that [Jer 10:9] הוּא כֶּסֶף מְרֻקָּע [מִ]תַּרְשִׁישׁ וּיֻבָא etc., [and Jer 10:10] אֱלֹהִים אֱמֶת ("[the Lord is] the true God").

For the prophets uttered these sayings only by way of marveling (al-taʿajjub), and of exposing the deficiency of those who take idols [as gods], and of calling attention to the evil of their choice — and that their affair, and the corruption of what they are upon, is not hidden from anyone who has in him the least grasp [of sense]; for were it the case that one of two things is more excellent than the other [only] by some slight thing, it would [still] be obligatory to choose the more excellent over that which is below it — how much the more when between the two [there is] this remote distance that has no limit, and when one of them is the loftiest of things and the highest of them, and the other the basest of things and the lowest of them, the meanest of them and the most shameful of them! So is it admissible, on the part of one possessed of sense, that he should not prefer this [Lord, the] lofty and most glorious over that base and most contemptible [idol]? And that is the counterpart of the saying of Isaiah [Isa 44:19] וְלֹא יָשִׁיב אֶל לִבּוֹ וְלֹא דַעַת [וְלֹא תְבוּנָה] ("and none lays it to heart, neither is there knowledge nor understanding").

For otherwise, how could what he said be sound, together with the rest of what he said of this kind? And likewise David (peace be upon him): when he said [Ps 135:5] כִּי אֲנִי יָדַעְתִּי כִּי גָדוֹל יְיָ וַאדֹנֵינוּ מִכָּל אֱלֹהִים ("for I know that the Lord is great, and our Lord [is] above all gods"), he followed that with a description of the greatness of the Creator's deeds (mighty and exalted), by his saying [Ps 135:6] כֹּל אֲשֶׁר חָפֵץ יְיָ עָשָׂה בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ ("whatever the Lord pleased He did, in heaven and on earth") and the rest of what he mentioned; then he took up the description of the idols, and their deficiency and their vileness, and said [Ps 135:15] עֲצַבֵּי הַגּוֹיִם כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב ("the idols of the nations are silver and gold") — and [thus] the [whole] meaning [is plain]; and this is evident.

: The third class of prooftext is the "the Lord is greater than all the gods" type (Exod 18:11; Jethro's confession). Q's first reply is an ad hominem retorsion: the doctrine's adherents argued (in Bab 19) that a thing can only be compared (yunqās) to what is near it in kind — but their own world-making angel is then incomparably above the idols (dead matter, man-made images), so the verse, on their principle, could no more be about a near-equal "Lord" than about anything else; the comparison-to-idols premise refutes them. The chain Jer 10:6-10 (none like the Lord … the idols are beaten silver … the Lord is the true God) shows Scripture's habitual juxtaposition of the incomparable God with worthless idols. : The constructive reply: the prophets' "greater than all gods" is not a ranking among comparable deities but a rhetorical figure — taʿajjub (marveling/astonishment) at the folly of idolatry, exposing how men prefer the basest thing (a fashioned image) to the loftiest (God). The a fortiori of preference (one would choose the more excellent even over a near-equal — all the more over an infinitely-distant inferior) drives home that the verses disparage idols, not rank God among gods. Isa 44:19 (the idol-maker "lays it not to heart … no knowledge, no understanding") is the locus classicus of the prophetic mockery of idolatry. The bracketed we-lo tevunah completes the verse, lost in the OCR (diff-report p174 i.27-28). : David's Ps 135 is adduced as the model of the figure: v. 5 ("the Lord is great, above all gods") is immediately unpacked by v. 6 (the Lord's cosmic deeds) and then contrasted with v. 15 (the gods of the nations are mere silver and gold) — so the "above all gods" is patently a foil for the idols' nullity, not a comparative ranking. The structure (assertion → divine omnipotence → idols' worthlessness) is Q's proof that the idiom is rhetorical throughout, and so yields nothing to the creator-angel reading.
§8 — To whom are prayer and praise directed?

8. Then they are asked about the prayers, the glorification, and the magnification (al-ṣalawāt wa-l-tasbīḥ wa-l-tamjīd): who is meant by that — the First Creator, or the angels? If they say "the angels," they have entered into the statement of the Sabians (al-Ṣābiʾīn), who alleged that they pray and offer worship to the stars in reverence for the Creator (mighty and exalted), since He is not [directly] reached, and since He has committed the governance of the world to the [celestial] sphere and the stars. So it follows for whoever holds [the doctrine] of the angels, if that is so — and [if] he were to pray and offer worship to the angels because God (mighty and exalted) committed to [the angel] the creation of the world — that he should pray also, and offer worship, to the stars, since their effect upon things is manifest and plain, and the sensory and rational proofs of that have stood firm, and their affair is more manifest than the affair of the angels.

And if they allege that they [in fact] pray and offer worship to the First Creator, then their statement concerning the angels is invalidated; for Scripture has reported, in more than one place, of the prayers of the prophets, that the One to whom they prayed is the One who created heaven and earth, and is the One who did all the deeds which they [the adherents] allege the angels did. Of that is the saying of David [Ps 136:1] הוֹדוּ לַייָ כִּי טוֹב כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ ("give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy endures forever"); and he says [Ps 136:2-3] הוֹדוּ לֵאלֹהֵי הָאֱלֹהִים ("give thanks to the God of gods"), and its completion [Ps 136:4] לְעֹשֵׂה נִפְלָאוֹת ("to Him who alone does wondrous things") to the end of the saying. And he says in Ezra [Neh 9:6] אַתָּה הוּא יְיָ לְבַדֶּךָ אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם ("You alone are the Lord; You made the heavens"), and its completion [Neh 9:7] אַתָּה הוּא יְיָ הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר בָּחַרְתָּ בְּאַבְרָם ("You are the Lord God who chose Abram") — and the rest of what they mentioned of that.

: The closing argument is a trilemma on the object of worship. If the adherents say prayer is to the angels, they collapse into the Ṣābiʾa (the Sabians, here the star-worshippers of Ḥarrān as the heresiographers depict them), whose rationale is identical — the transcendent God being unreachable, worship is offered to the heavenly governors He appointed; and worse, Q presses, on that logic they ought to worship the stars too, whose causal influence is even more "manifest" than the angels'. If, on the other hand, they say prayer is to the First Creator, then they concede precisely what the doctrine denies — that the maker of heaven and earth, the doer of "all the deeds they ascribe to the angels," is the one God to whom the prophets prayed: David's hodu la-YHWH … le-ʿoseh niflaʾot le-vaddo (Ps 136, the Great Hallel, "to Him who alone does wonders") and Nehemiah's attah hu YHWH le-vaddekha attah ʿasita et ha-shamayim (Neh 9:6, "You alone … You made the heavens"). The repeated le-vaddo / le-vaddekha ("alone") is the scriptural hammer: creation is the unshared act of the one God. Note that Q (following his own and the medieval convention) cites Nehemiah under the rubric עֶזְרָא (Ezra-Nehemiah being a single book). The bab ends here, at the foot of p173.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is bare — fī al-radd ʿalayhim, "on the refutation of them" — and is intelligible only from Bab 19, which set out the doctrine of a group holding that the world was created not by God directly but by an exalted angel (al-malʾak) to whom creation was delegated. The position is a creator-intermediary/demiurge doctrine; Q explicitly aligns its rationale with the dualism of the Mannāniyya (Manichaeans, §4) and its cultic consequence with the Ṣābiʾa (star-worshipping Sabians, §8). Whether Q regards the adherents as a Jewish sect, a Christian-adjacent group, or a philosophical current is left unstated in this bab; the demiurge-and-intermediary structure is gnosticizing, and the explicit Manichaean/Sabian comparisons situate it among the dualist and astral-cult heresies of the kalām heresiographers.

- Two registers of refutation, mirroring Babs 5–6. As in the anti-Christian babs, Q splits the refutation into a rational half (§§1–4) and a scriptural-philological half (§§5–8), the second neutralizing the opponents' prooftext-catalogue (laid out in Bab 19) verse by verse. The rational half is the more original: §1's fallacy-of-the-inverse on the differentia, §2's all-or-one dilemma, §3's reductio that the interposed angel destroys the cosmological proof of God's eternity, and §4's demonstration that the only available (dualist) motive for delegation is self-defeating because God creates by will, not by contact.

- The exegetical key (§5): outward speaker ≠ real agent. The scriptural half turns on a single philological principle — that prophetic and angelic first-person speech routinely voices what is in reality God's deed and speech (the angel's "I will multiply your seed" = God's; Moses' "I will be with you" = God's; Elijah's "I bring evil" = God's). This dissolves the "an angel said/did X as God" prooftexts (§5) without conceding the angel is creator; §6 adds the agency principle (God sends angels — and humans — as deliverers, but sending an agent ≠ delegating creation); §7 the rhetoric-of-wonder principle (the "greater than all gods" verses disparage idols, they do not rank deities); §8 the object-of-worship trilemma.

- The Manichaean and Sabian tags. Q's two heresiographical comparisons are load-bearing, not decorative. The Mannāniyya tag (§4) identifies the doctrine's hidden premise (matter is intrinsically base, so the Pure One delegates its making) as crypto-dualism. The Ṣābiʾa tag (§8) identifies its cultic upshot (worship of an appointed intermediary because God is unreachable) as crypto-astrolatry — and Q sharpens it into a slippery-slope: by the same reasoning the adherents should worship the stars, whose causal efficacy is even more evident.
